beats.narration: The connected firmware is finished. It has Wi-Fi, encryption, signed updates, a display, and a history log. There is just one problem.
The linker says the program is nine kilobytes too big for the flash. And RAM is over by six hundred bytes.
So buy a bigger chip.
The boards are already designed, and five thousand chips are already ordered. We are not buying a bigger chip.
We are going to make this program smaller, and faster while we are at it.
This is a classic embedded moment. The hardware is fixed. The features are promised. And the only way forward is to understand exactly where every byte and every microsecond goes.
Step one is not guessing. It is measuring. And the tool for measuring memory is the map file the linker writes every time it builds.
Code goes in the text section. Constant data, like strings and tables, in read-only data.
Initialized variables need space twice: their starting values in flash, and the variables themselves in RAM. Zero-initialized variables only need RAM.
The map file also lists every function and variable with its size. Sort that list, and the biggest offenders jump out.
Printf? Seven kilobytes for printing text?
A full printf handles every format, including floating point. We barely use it. That is our first target.
First, the compiler. Optimizing for size instead of speed often saves ten to twenty percent immediately. Combined with link-time optimization, the linker can also discard functions nobody calls.

beats.narration: Second, libraries. A single call to a floating point function can drag in kilobytes of software math routines on a chip without a floating point unit.

beats.narration: RAM is often tighter than flash, and harder to measure, because the stack and the heap change while the program runs.
Globals are visible in the map file. The stack is not.
We measure it with the watermark trick from the bugs episode: fill it with a pattern at boot, run everything hard, then check how much pattern survived.
The stack had two kilobytes reserved, but the peak use was one point one.
That spare can be reclaimed, carefully, leaving a safety margin for code paths the test might not have hit.
Sharing buffers is a big one. The network receive buffer and the display frame buffer are never busy at the same time, because we turn the display off during uploads.

Use smaller types for small numbers
Pack flags into bits

beats.narration: The cryptography library wants to allocate memory dynamically, with malloc. Many embedded teams avoid dynamic allocation entirely. Ada explains why.
Allocate and free blocks of different sizes over time, and free memory gets chopped into small, scattered pieces.
There may be plenty free in total, but no single piece big enough. That is fragmentation.
On a desktop, a failed allocation is rare and the operating system has tricks.
On a microcontroller running for months, a slowly fragmenting heap is a time bomb with a very long fuse.
Our approach: allocate everything the crypto library needs at boot, once, and never free it. If it fits on day one, it fits on day five hundred.

visual.title: Safer alternatives
items: Allocate everything once at startup
Use fixed-size memory pools
Use static buffers sized for the worst case
If you must use a heap, never free, or free in reverse order

beats.narration: And memory pools for messages. Every message buffer is exactly the same size, so any free buffer fits any request. No fragmentation possible.

beats.narration: Next problem. The watering screen feels sluggish. Pressing a key takes nearly half a second to update the display. Cy calls it, the sleepy keypad.
Before optimizing anything, we profile. Guessing where time goes is wrong surprisingly often.
The simplest method is the debug pin: set it high at the start of a function, low at the end, and look at the scope.

visual.title: Profiling tools
items: Toggle a pin, measure with a scope
Read a cycle counter before and after
Sample the program counter periodically
Count how often functions run

beats.narration: The width of the pulse is the time.

beats.narration: Many processors also have a cycle counter, a register that counts every clock cycle. Reading it before and after a block of code gives a precise duration, without a scope.

beats.narration: Point four seconds to redraw the screen? That is the whole delay!
A third method, statistical profiling, interrupts the program thousands of times per second and records where the program counter is.
Functions that appear in many samples are where time is spent.
The redraw calls draw pixel one point one million times per screen. Each call computes the pixel's address, checks bounds, and sets one bit.
The fix is not to make draw pixel faster. It is to stop calling it so often. Most of the screen is unchanged between frames.

beats.narration: And whole bytes can be written at once instead of single bits.

visual.title: The slow inner loop

beats.narration: First, redraw only regions that changed. Second, write eight pixels per byte instead of one. Third, send rows using DMA instead of the processor.

visual.title: Optimization, in order of payoff
items: Do less: skip work that is not needed
Choose a better algorithm
Move work out of inner loops
Use the hardware: DMA, bigger transfers
Only then: micro-tune the code

beats.narration: From four hundred milliseconds to six. The keypad wakes up. And notice: not a single trick involved clever assembly. Doing less and using the hardware beat micro-optimization by a mile.
Sixty-six times faster! I am putting that in the next pitch deck.
You put the six microseconds in the last pitch deck.
There is a balance between speed and size. Techniques that make code faster, like unrolling loops or inlining functions, often make it bigger.
Techniques that make it smaller can make it slower.
The trick is to apply speed optimizations only to the few functions that the profile says are hot, and optimize everything else for size. Most code runs rarely.
It should be small. A tiny fraction runs constantly. It should be fast.
Once the big wins are taken, a few smaller habits still help in hot code.
Using the natural word size matters on thirty-two bit processors.

visual.title: Small habits for hot code
items: Use the processor's natural word size
Avoid division in loops; precompute
Keep data together in memory
Use lookup tables for repeated math
Read the compiler's output for the hottest loop

beats.narration: An eight bit loop counter can force extra instructions to wrap it at two hundred fifty-five, while a thirty-two bit one is free.
